title: PyShim park/unpark tokenization handoff exploratory notes
content:
Summary:

We reproduced a recurring production spike where small requests (<= 160 tokens) show unexpectedly high tail latency despite low GPU time. Hypothesis: CPU-side tokenization + request-parse + thread handoff (park/unpark) overhead dominates total wall time for short requests. This doc collects sampling runs, microbenchmarks, flame graph observations, tentative root-cause, and prioritized mitigations to try.

Environment and harness:

- Image: runtime-docker:2025-01-xx (glibc 2.36, Linux 5.15 kernel in tests)
- Python: CPython 3.11.4 built with clang, jemalloc enabled in smoke runs
- Tokenizers tested: HuggingFace Tokenizers (Rust tokenizer via Python bindings), sentencepiece (C++), and a pure-Python fallback used by tests to exaggerate GIL effects
- Network driver: host-mode TCP sockets (wrk-compatible client) inside same AZ to minimize network jitter
- Load pattern: single connection, 600 rps sustained, requests sampled at uniform inter-arrival times; payloads: short prompts (avg 60 chars), medium (250 chars)
- Microbenchmarks run pinned to one NUMA node, isolated CPUs via cset for reproducibility

Methodology:

1) Sampled Python processes with 100Hz async-sample profiler (statically compiled py-spy) during end-to-end requests and produced flame graphs for main & worker threads.
2) Traced syscalls via perf trace and strace for a subset to confirm park/unpark and futex patterns.
3) Measured context switch counts via /proc/<pid>/status and perf stat.
4) Built synthetic microbench: tokenization-only loop + small JSON parse + handoff to worker thread through a Python ThreadPoolExecutor wrapper to measure handoff latency.

Key findings (high level):

- Tokenization CPU cost itself is modest for native tokenizers (Rust/C++): ~200-400 us per short prompt.
- However, observed additional 0.6–1.4 ms per request in context switch+thread-wakeup cost when using our default thread pool and request parsing path. This is the dominant overhead for short requests.

Flame graph observations:

- Main thread stack frequently shows: recvmsg -> read -> json.loads (C) -> submit-to-threadpool (Python) -> wait for Future.result (futex)
- Worker threads show: futex_wait -> park (pthread_cond_wait) -> tokenizer C/Rust binding (releasing GIL briefly) -> futex_wake -> Python callback path
- A hotspot appears around the cross-thread synchronization primitives; the handoff pattern in our code performs a submit and then a blocking wait on the result on the main event-handling thread (synchronous handoff).

Syscall and kernel-level signals:

- perf trace shows many futex wake/wait pairs per request. For small payloads this averages ~6 futex events per request (submit, wake, wait for callback, signal to main thread, etc.).
- Context switches (voluntary + involuntary) increase by ~40–60 per second per core under the 600 rps workload vs. baseline; per-request estimate ~0.7 context switches, matches latency overhead.

Microbenchmark numbers (representative):

- Native HF tokenizer (Rust binding): 250 us median per call; pure-Python tokenizer: 2.6 ms median
- JSON parse (C library): 80–120 us median
- Synchronous handoff using ThreadPoolExecutor + Future.result (small closure): 900–1400 us added latency (median depends on scheduling)
- Pipelined (non-blocking) approach with callback + queue: 150–300 us added latency (much better for bursts)

Hypotheses refined:

1) The synchronous submit+wait pattern on the main thread causes unnecessary park/unpark churn and blocks the event loop while worker threads are scheduled in and out; this is painful for short requests where CPU kernels are tiny.

2) Even with tokenizer implemented in native code that briefly releases the GIL, the cost of thread wakeups and Python-level synchronization dominates for <1ms CPU operations.

3) The standard ThreadPoolExecutor has poor wake-up characteristics for very fine-grained tasks: the submit-then-block idiom turns short CPU tasks into multiple kernel transitions.

Exploratory mitigations and quick experiments attempted:

A) Batch tokenization at ingress (combine requests for few ms window): improved tail latency for bursts but increased median for single-request latency. Good for throughput-oriented endpoints; not ideal for strict P99 SLOs targeting low latency.

B) Move tokenization into async-compatible native extension that performs tokenization in-place and returns PyBuffer without handing work to separate threads. Implemented a tiny C extension prototype that calls tokenizer C API while holding GIL only for object conversions; result: removed one futex/wakeup pair and reduced per-request overhead by ~350–500 us on short requests.

C) Switch to dedicated pinned worker pool (one per CPU core, pre-started threads pinned to CPUs) to avoid scheduler jitter. This reduced worst-case handoff latency variability (less out-of-order scheduling) and shaved ~150–300 us P95. Costs: higher baseline thread count and memory, more complex lifecycle on autoscaling.

D) Replace blocking Future.result path with lock-free ring buffer and a notification fd (eventfd) + epoll integration to let main loop wait on eventfd rather than futex. Proof-of-concept lowered wakeup latency and reduced syscalls per request.

E) Try io_uring for socket reads to reduce wakeups on network path (not yet benchmarked end-to-end).

Tradeoffs observed:

- Aggressive batching reduces wakeups but increases added latency for single requests.
- Pinning threads reduces jitter but increases resource cost and complicates deployment in multi-tenant nodes.
- Native extension approach gives best single-request latency improvement with modest engineering effort but needs safe lifetime & memory management reviews (we must avoid leaking buffers across tenants).

Prioritized next steps (what to try in short term):

1) Implement production-grade native tokenization shim (small C extension) that performs tokenization without threadpool handoff. Owner: Owen. Ticket: SRV-1127. Target: prototype in 1 week, safety review in 2 weeks.

2) Replace blocking submit/wait on main thread with epoll-waitable notification (eventfd) to reduce futex wakes in the hot path. Owner: Sophie. Ticket: SRV-1133. Target: experiment + perf numbers in 10 days.

3) Add pinned worker pool option behind a runtime flag for dedicated instances; run soak tests with pinned pool to measure memory and throughput impact. Owner: Diego. Ticket: SRV-1135. Target: POC in 2 weeks.

4) Add microbench for park/unpark measurement to CI perf suite: make it possible to detect regressions when we change submit patterns. Owner: Maya. Ticket: SRV-1141. Target: CI addition in 1 week.

Longer-term investigation items:

- Evaluate subinterpreters (PEP 554 family) for isolation and lower scheduling overhead (contrasted with GIL complexity). Past experiments in repo show mixed results; revisit with new 3.11 capabilities.
- Consider moving the entire request parsing + tokenization to a Rust-based service (sidecar) for extremely latency-sensitive routes. Adds O(1) network latency but reduces park/unpark inside main process.
- Explore io_uring for socket ingestion to measure reductions in syscalls and wakeups under small-payload workloads.

Open questions / unknowns:

- How much of the observed futex traffic is from third-party libraries (e.g., logging, metrics exporter) vs. our hot path? Need a filtered perf trace to answer.
- Nightly kernel behavior: are there scheduler tunables (RT priorities, wake-up preemption settings) we can tweak safely in shared environments?
- Quantify memory/cost impact of pinned thread pools across all instance sizes.

Appendix: quick reproducer (local):

- tiny harness in repo: experiments/park-unpark-repro/ contains: simple TCP server (uvloop) -> main thread receives request -> json.loads -> executor.submit(tokenize) -> future.result() -> write response. Use wrk with 600 rps and short payload.
- Scripts: run_bench.sh (pins cpus, toggles jemalloc), capture_flame.sh (py-spy record --native), compare.sh (produce folded stacks).

Notes to reviewers:

- This doc is intentionally exploratory and contains rough numbers. Please run reproducer in your dev machines pinned to the same kernel version for the closest match.
- If you own a change that affects the request submit path (agent, middleware, or providers SDK), please scan for submit+block idioms and avoid synchronous waits on the main handler thread.

Action items (short):

- Create SRV-1127 (native tokenizer shim) [Owen]
- Create SRV-1133 (epoll notification integration) [Sophie]
- Create SRV-1135 (pinned worker pool option) [Diego]
- Add CI microbench for park/unpark (Maya)

-- Maya
